sourceEvidence.label: Wardrowbe auth, deployment, and outbound HTTP source review

assessment.summary: One shared outbound-authority boundary can address global TLS weakening, destination SSRF risk, and credential forwarding drift.

nonNegotiables: Run on a weak Linux server
assumptions: No measured latency or memory budget was supplied.

opportunities.title: Own outbound destination, TLS, and credential policy
opportunities.summary: Route security-sensitive HTTP calls through one policy that validates every destination and binds credentials to administrative trust.
opportunities.diagnosis: TLS and destination controls are owned by deployment flags and individual callers, while user-controlled URLs can reach server network authority.

evidence.claim: Frontend sets NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED=0 for all Node HTTPS requests.
User-configured AI URLs are called with redirects enabled and the server-wide AI API key.
User-configured notification destinations reach redirect-following HTTP clients without address-class policy.
Existing provider-specific CA support can replace global TLS weakening without redesigning OIDC.

desiredInvariants: Every security-sensitive HTTPS connection verifies a trusted certificate chain.
Every outbound destination and redirect hop is resolved and checked against an explicit policy before connection.
A server credential is sent only to an administrator-owned destination explicitly bound to that credential.

options.title: Owned in-process outbound boundary
options.summary: Centralize validation and client construction in backend/frontend helpers, using scoped CA trust and per-destination credentials.

evidenceCoverage.rationale: Remove global TLS disable and configure provider CA trust.
Validate destinations and stop sending ambient API keys.
Shared checks cover known channels; each provider still needs integration tests.

tradeoffs.assessment: Known callers gain fail-closed destination and credential checks, though future callers can bypass the helper.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Run private-address, DNS rebinding, redirect, CA, and credential-leak tests across every caller.

tradeoffs.assessment: DNS resolution and redirect validation add bounded work before outbound calls.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Measure p50/p95 request setup time for AI and notification calls.

tradeoffs.assessment: Policy state and resolved-address sets remain small.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Compare backend RSS during concurrent outbound requests.

tradeoffs.assessment: Bad destinations fail before connection, but DNS edge cases can reject previously working private endpoints.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Test approved private endpoints on IPv4, IPv6, and Tailscale.

tradeoffs.assessment: No new service; allowlist and rejection logs need ownership.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Exercise configuration, observability, and incident runbooks.

tradeoffs.assessment: Existing API shapes can remain while unsafe destinations become validation errors.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Run compatibility tests for approved OIDC, AI, ntfy, and Mattermost endpoints.

residualRisks: Callers outside the owned helper can reintroduce ambient authority.
Application-level validation cannot contain a compromised process.

acceptanceCriteria: Untrusted TLS and forbidden address classes fail closed
Global keys never reach user-owned destinations
migrationNotes: Allowlist intended local AI endpoints explicitly
implementationReadiness.rollback: Revert shared client use while retaining global TLS verification.

options.title: Dedicated outbound egress gateway
options.summary: Move destination enforcement and credentials to a constrained proxy; application workloads receive no direct sensitive egress authority.

evidenceCoverage.rationale: Frontend OIDC still needs correct CA trust; gateway protects backend egress.
Gateway owns allowed AI destinations and credentials.
Network boundary blocks direct notification egress.

tradeoffs.assessment: Network isolation reduces bypass and credential blast radius, but the gateway becomes privileged.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Prove backend direct egress fails and gateway policy rejects forbidden targets and redirects.

tradeoffs.assessment: One network hop and possible request buffering are added.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Compare AI streaming and notification latency through the gateway.

tradeoffs.assessment: An additional process and connection pools consume memory.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Measure idle and peak gateway RSS on target weak server.

tradeoffs.assessment: Gateway failure can stop all outbound features, though it also contains failures.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Run restart, timeout, saturation, and rollback drills.

tradeoffs.assessment: New deployment, policy, logs, health checks, and upgrades are required.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Operate a staging gateway through one upgrade and incident exercise.

tradeoffs.assessment: All outbound callers and network policies must move together or through a staged compatibility mode.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Canary one channel, then AI calls, with direct-egress monitoring before enforcement.

residualRisks: Frontend OIDC TLS remains outside backend gateway.
Gateway policy or credential compromise remains high impact.

acceptanceCriteria: Backend cannot connect directly to forbidden networks
migrationNotes: Canary by channel before default-deny egress
implementationReadiness.rollback: Restore direct egress and remove gateway routing while preserving application validation.

opportunities.recommendation: Use the in-process boundary for the private family phase; move to a gateway if public multi-user risk or compliance requirements outweigh weak-server constraints.

openQuestions: Which private AI hosts must family deployment allow?
Will public users configure their own outbound destinations?
